20-Year-Old Drives Rare Chevy Caprice, Wants Everything Impala SS on It, Says It Won't Be a Clone
14 photos
Photo: Pomeroy's Garage | YouTube
A young man from Ontario bought a rust-free, rare 1996 Chevrolet Caprice B4U. While it might be the kind of car that a grandma would drive, he loves the attention that the classic sedan brings him. Because he loves Impala SSs, he plans to swap a thing or two (or more), but promises: "I won't turn it into an Impala SS clone!"
Young people usually chase after the newest cars with the latest tech. This guy, however, is into classic cars and hunts the best deals. John Pomeroy , who is only 20 years old, drives cars that are sometimes double his age or more.
His latest purchase is a 30-year-old Chevy Caprice B4U he bought for $5,000 CAD, which translates to roughly US$3,490. " An amazing steal ," he says. That’s not entirely true. While low-mileage, well-preserved examples can fetch around US$10,000 at auctions, cars that are not exactly garage queens rarely go over the US $5,000 mark.
However, he is going to spend some more money on a makeover. He absolutely loves Chevy Impala SSs and plans to make the Caprice a bit sportier without turning it into an Impala SS clone. That sounds like a promise he won’t be able to keep.
Photo: Pomeroy's Garage | YouTube The B4U is a rare, factory-optioned performance package that gave the Caprice sedans the mechanical hardware of the iconic Impala SS without the sporty appearance, making it the ultimate sleeper. Unofficial reports indicate that roughly 9,064 B4U Chevy Caprices were built for the model year
While the 1994 - 1996 Impala SS featured monochromatic paint, a rear spoiler, bucket seats, and 17-inch wheels, a B4U Caprice kept its chrome trim, wire hubcaps or standard alloys, hood ornament, and front bench seat.
Because the Impala SS and the Chevy Caprice B4U shared the exact same LT1 and heavy-duty underpinnings, the Caprice delivered nearly identical acceleration and highway cruising power at a fraction of the price of the Impala SS.
1996 was the final year of the fourth-generation B-body Caprice. That year, ordering the B4U option was the only way to get the range-topping powertrain in a non-police civilian sedan. In addition to the LT1 V8, the car came with the FE3 sport suspension, the V08 heavy-duty cooling, a limited-slip differential, and a dual exhaust system.
Photo: Pomeroy's Garage | YouTube He bought the body-on-frame sedan out of Texas, so it comes rust-free, has never even been driven in winter, and has never seen salt. Things are probably about to change in Ontario, Canada, where Pomeroy lives, but he plans to take care of it so that it drives 30 more years.
Finished in Adriatic Blue, which John says is one of his all-time favorite colors, along with black and white on these Caprices. It came with minor dings and dents, but overall, it is in great condition, considering its age, and has some of the most desirable features of its era.
The Caprice B4U rides on Impala five-spoke Chevy Impala wheels, but Pomeroy would love a set of N97 9C1s. However, he is going to swap them for OZ Racing wheels that he used to have on his 1985 Buick LeSabre. An Impala trunk lid with a little spoiler will replace the original one.
The factory taillights will be out, and Impala units will be in. John also intends to switch to an Impala SS rear end with disc brakes all around and plans to get rid of the purple rear window tints. Those tints protect a cabin that is in far worse condition than the exterior, which is far from abnormal at 123,000 miles (197,949 kilometers).
Photo: Pomeroy's Garage | YouTube The leather steering wheel is peeling off, and the driver’s seat is split open. The dashboard is cracked, but the new owner has a spare one to replace the factory dash. The good news that the door panels are in good condition. Everything works on board.
The 1996 Caprice features power seats, power mirrors, and the very rare optional Twilight Sentinel, General Motors' automatic headlight and exit-lighting system, which automatically turns the exterior lights on at dusk, turns them off in bright daylight, and keeps them lit briefly after the driver parks it so that they can walk to their door at night.
Pomeroy is planning to replace the factory seats with Bonneville seats up front and Impala seats out back. As for the cargo space, " t his is a seven-body trunk ," says the new owner of the Caprice. He probably watched too many crime movies.
At the opposite end, under the long hood, which John wants to replace with an SLP Ram Air hood, sits the 5.7-liter LT1 V8, derived from the Corvette . The V8 produces 260 horsepower (264 metric horsepower) and 330 pound-feet (447 Newton meters) of torque. That makes it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 7.2 seconds on its way to a top speed of 135 mph (217 kph).
With everything he plans to modify on the car, it doesn’t sound like a Chevy Impala SS clone. It sounds like the Impala SS itself.

New Owner Repaints All-Original 1969 Camaro Z/28 Time Capsule, Internet Is Enraged, He Sells It
68 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Classic car restorations have a notorious habit of stretching across years, sometimes dragging on for decades while parts gather dust and owners lose patience. Parked beneath the bright lights of the 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals in Rosemont, Illinois, however, sat a dazzling LeMans Blue 1969 Chevrolet Camaro Z/28 that defied every shop cliché.
Finished for showtime in just 10 hard days, this matching-numbers pony car proved that speed and concours precision can coexist. First of all, the car didn’t actually need the repaint; the original livery was showing signs of wear and rust was creeping up here and there, but it wasn’t a case of “It must be done before it is too far gone.” Not by a long shot. Still, some gearheads are absolutely maniacal with their standards. Mr. Autobody is among them.
Automotive chronicler Lou Costabile spotted the blue standout on the floor of the Donald E. Stephens Convention Center during the traditional weekend before Thanksgiving showcase. The car’s former owner, Chris Moffitt, proprietor of Mr. Auto Body in Champaign, Illinois, did the work on it in record time. With over 50 years of bodywork heritage, the shop focuses almost exclusively on 1969 Camaro Z/28 restorations.
Moffitt acquired this particular Z/28 around February 2026 and brought it back to his Illinois facility, where it sat untouched for a while. At the time, the coupe still wore its factory-applied paint, and virtually everyone who inspected it urged him to preserve the survivor finish. See the second video for the initial condition of this stunner pony car.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile After staring at the sheet metal for a long stretch, though, Moffitt made his call: the car simply had to be restored because it would look breathtaking once finished.
Once committed, the 10-strong crew attacked the Camaro relentlessly for 10 hard days, fitting Mr. Auto Body's usual two-week pace plus another five days for final touch-ups. The team documented this LeMans Blue coupe's rebuild on social media, tackling quarter-panel metalwork and sanding against a tight clock for John Clay Wolfe's Throttlefest in Walnut Springs, Texas, before heading to MCACN.
Moffitt refuses solo credit whenever admirers ask who painted or built the Camaro. Rather than drowning in deadline stress, his shop throws collective manpower—or horsepower, as he jokes—at each project as a tight-knit team having genuine fun. That high-velocity formula already produced a 10-day Olympic Gold 1969 RS Z/28 that set a Mecum Auctions record earlier in 2026, while a partially assembled Daytona Yellow Z/28 joined this blue coupe on display at MCACN.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile What elevates the rapid turnaround is how faithfully the coupe preserves its original hardware. Beneath the cowl-induction hood sits the matching-numbers 302-cubic-inch Turbo-Fire V8, backed by its original Muncie M21 close-ratio 4-speed manual and factory rear axle (4.10 gears).
Dressed in LeMans Blue with white stripes, spoilers, and 15x7 Rally wheels wearing Goodyear Wide Tread F70-15 tires, the coupe retains its scarce smog equipment and spatter-painted trunk with factory decals.
The black interior remains completely factory original , from the headliner to the bucket seats still showing their telltale white stitching, alongside a console with four gauges, a Hurst shifter, an in-dash tachometer, a clock, and a Delco AM radio. Underhood, Moffitt's crew reproduced documented assembly-line markings—including orange “PTB” (Paint Trim Body) stencils and “M21” firewall chalk—plus Moffitt's personal “22” signature on the fan shroud.
Photo: YouTube/Mr. Auto Body (@mr.autobody) Blistering build times aim squarely at attracting young people to classic cars. Young apprentices quickly grow bored watching a project linger for years; in Moffitt's shop, they experience the thrill of watching a legend transform from teardown to finish in days. If ever there was a more practical example of how the age of high-speed internet and instant gratification (read “speed shopping online”) has altered the human behavior, this would be it.
That urgency befits one of Detroit's fiercest nameplates. Chevrolet introduced the Camaro in September 1966 for the 1967 model year on General Motors' F-body platform to duel the Ford Mustang. Across six generations spanning two eras—first from 1967 to 1969, second through 1981, third through 1992, fourth through 2002, fifth on the Zeta platform from 2010 to 2015, and sixth on the Alpha chassis from 2016 until December 2023—Chevrolet built over 5.5 million Camaros.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Collectors still prize the first generation above all others, encompassing 220,906 units in 1967, 235,147 in 1968, and 243,085 in the prolonged 15-month 1969 production year. Conceived by Vince Piggins to homologate Chevrolet for SCCA Trans-Am racing, the track-bred Z/28 debuted quietly with just 602 examples in 1967 before climbing to 7,199 in 1968. By 1969, street and circuit dominance had made the badge famous, pushing Z/28 production to an impressive 20,302 coupes.
Chevrolet created the Z/28's high-revving 302-cubic-inch (4.9-liter) V8 by pairing a 327 V8 block's 4.00-inch bore with a 283 V8 crankshaft's 3.00-inch stroke, adding solid lifters, forged internals, and 11.0:1 compression. It came conservatively rated at 290 hp at 5,800 rpm and 290 lb-ft at 4,200 rpm (294 PS, 393 Nm, but I think those figures applied to the first six cylinders).
It required a 4-speed manual, heavy-duty suspension, and front discs. Period tests logged 0-60 mph in 7.1 to 7.4 seconds and a 133-mph top speed. When new in 1969, a base V8 Camaro sport coupe cost $2,726 before rising to $2,727 in January, while the RPO Z28 package added $458.15 early on and climbed to $522.40 late in the run, putting base Z/28 pricing near $3,185 before required options.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Today, Classic.com places the 1969 Z/28 market benchmark at $103,003, while BidBetter tracks a $90,001 median across 333 auctions, with typical sales spanning $68,000 to $115,000. Speaking of prices, this Le Mans Blue time capsule is sold (hence, why I referred to Chris Moffitt as “Former Owner”).
It sparked some adverse reactions from gearheads strongly demanding to keep the car original. I am on the fence about this – I like how it looks right now, but I also know that they can’t be original more than once. You be the judge – watch the two videos embedded below and let me know in the comments which version of the car you prefer.
Top documented 1969 Camaro Z/28 examples have reached a $330,000 auction record, including a headline sale at Mecum Kissimmee in 2026. Across the entire Camaro nameplate, the all-time crown belongs to the 1969 COPO Yenko Camaro prototype, which hammered to $1,815,000 with buyer's premium at Mecum Kissimmee in January 2026—underscoring why Moffitt's 10-day LeMans Blue marvel could not have possibly gone unnoticed in Rosemont.

EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
What the Heck Happened To Car Interiors and Why Physical Controls Matter
13 photos
Photo: BMW | Autoevolution
Ask petrolheads what they really think of new cars and most of them will tell you that the entire industry today is an absolute mess.
Everyone is in this game for one reason and one reason only: to make money. And guess where they’re making it from? That’s right, from new car buyers. One might think that as a result, companies would be more open to listening to what their clients want. But most of them aren’t. And that’s why we now have some quirky designs when it comes to certain automakers, not mention screen-filled interiors, fewer physical controls, and lots of plastic.
Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you know that there is no major difference anymore between mainstream and premium cars. And the line becomes almost invisible when you opt for range-topping versions of the former, as leather upholstery, even if it may be fake, or artificial as companies like to call it, some cool trim, and additional gizmos tend to trick the eye into thinking that companies such as Mazda, Toyota, Peugeot, Renault, and so on have entered the premium game.
By the way, there isn’t anything particularly wrong with these brands. They just came to mind first. But there is something very wrong with premium companies. Every petrolhead and their pet knows that Mercedes’ vehicles are not what they used to be. They’re not built like tanks anymore , and that I can understand, because an unbreakable machine means less money to be made from the servicing part. But squeaky interiors with lots of plastics, and screens that jiggle in cars that cost six digits is a major no-no.
Photo: BMW I know from a reliable source that Mercedes had to save money a few years ago, and instead of jumping on the layover bandwagon, they decided to cut from the quality of their cars. And they’re not the only ones, because companies that make far superior machines such as Rolls-Royce have also done that. And this reminds me of a particular Ghost that I drove a few years ago. It cost the equivalent of $400,000 back then, and car crickets were a thing.
Excuse me, what did I just say? That’s not a typo, as squeaky full-size luxury sedans are still a thing today. And if companies such as Rolls-Royce can get away with it, then so can premium brands. Mercedes is the best example here, but let’s admit it, it’s not like its two main German rivals, namely Audi and BMW, are that far behind. I’m more familiar with the latter rather than the former for subjective reasons, as I have always been a BMW fan, and I’m now on my third Bimmer.
But that does not matter in this story, as I have ventured a bit too far from the initial topic, which revolves around interiors. And for subjective reasons, I’ve decided to compare the cockpits of a not-so-old Bimmer with a brand new one. In the opening image, you can see the F10 BMW 5 Series LCI . Why this model? Because that’s what I drive. Notice how the infotainment system is neatly integrated into the dashboard panel?
How about the fact that it has a digital instrument cluster that looks like an analogue one? The air vents are on the traditional side of things, you get read controls for the sound system, and physical buttons and knobs to control the HVAC system. In my BMW, I can adjust the temperature, turn on the seat heating, and do all kind of things without taking my eyes off the road simply by pushing buttons and turning knobs.
That’s mission impossible when it comes to the later models, namely the Neue Klasse ones. Since there is no new Neue Klasse BMW 5 Series yet, I’ve compared the interior of the F10 with that of the G50 3 Series . And it’s not comparing apples and oranges, because this is exactly what the cockpit of the G6X LCI will look like. With the same Panoramic iDrive, the free-floating infotainment screen, the quirky-looking steering wheel, and so on.
Photo: BMW Sure, there will be a few differences between the interiors of the upcoming 5er and that of the new 3er, but overall, it’s pretty much the same recipe. A giant screen used to control everything, and a pillar-to-pillar display stretching at the bottom of the windscreen. And yes, you could control certain things by talking to the car, but let’s imagine a scenario.
It’s 5 to 10 years from now, and you were finally able to upgrade from your old Bimmer to a newer one. The winner is a Neue Klasse , let’s say a 5er. You are cruising the road delighted with the extra tech features when all of a sudden, the main screen goes dark. The car does not talk back to you anymore, and you cannot adjust the interior temperature, not to mention do all kinds of things. Would you still want the button-less interior then?
On top of that, it’s always been common sense in the car world to make ergonomically-friendly vehicles, but the modern ones are not exactly that, are they? In fact, most of them feel like smartphones on wheels, and let’s compare a modern-day smartphone with one made 5 to 10 years ago. Which one would you rather have? Thus, unless I am missing something, there won’t be a big demand for new-age cars on the used market a few years from now.
I’ve always been a fan of more traditional interiors rather than tech-filled ones, and I definitely hate the screen fest that the automotive world is heading into. What’s wrong with pushing a button and turning a knob? Do we really want to tap screens for everything? Where does the safety part fit? What about the reliability? Will we be able to look at today’s cars 30 years from now like we do at vehicles made in the 1990s and say that they were made to last?
Then again, this is a major problem in every field today, as everything feels like it was made to break easily. And the same goes for cars. So, from a petrolhead’s perspective, do you dig the button-less trend in modern-day rides?

Pontiac Firebird Trans Am Spent Over 40 Years Abandoned in a Closed Dealership, Now It's Finally Out
22 photos
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube
This 1978 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am was traded in at 2,000 miles with a mechanical issue. The dealership shop slapped a band-aid on it and was planning to sell it quickly. However, the dealership closed, and the car remained abandoned at the back of the shop.
1978 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am sat abandoned in a closed dealership in a small town in Georgia. The service manager tried to sell the car, but it never actually made it to the showroom. It just sat in the back, hidden away from the eyes of the customers until the dealership was permanently shut down. Now, Vagner Moleiro of Percepcar USA bought it for $15,000.
The car had been brought in as a trade-in at just 2,000 miles and got a patchwork fix. Then, over the years, it just sat there, untouched, collecting dust instead of miles, and grime that hid away the Trans Am's typical black and gold paint scheme .
The entire lower section is covered in mud, which is a hint that the car wasn't even washed before it entered service over 40 years ago. The cabin is covered in dry mud and debris, like this car spent its entire life on a construction site. Now, power washing reveals a black paint that has gone dull. But clay barring and polishing every inch of the Firebird will work miracles.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube General Motors phased out Hurst Hatches around mid-1978 in favor of its own Fisher T-tops, which were the factory T-top roof style for 1979 T rans Ams . Hurst panels are smaller (roughly 30.25" × 17.5"), leaving about 16 inches of center roof structure between them. Meanwhile, the Fisher panels are larger (about 33.5" × 22.25"), leaving about 6 inches between them.
In 1978, Pontiac rolled out 3,643 Firebird Trans Ams in Black and Gold. Of the 3,643, only 298 units featured the Fisher T-Tops. Of the 298, only 88 of them had the 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) V8 under the hood like this Trans Am, which makes it incredibly rare and definitely worth saving. “I’m not going to be the one who loses one that way,” Vagner says.
Now, 48 years later, the price tag is still dangling from the mirror. He bought for cheap a car that would normally be around $80,000 and can cross the $100,000 mark in top condition. In 1978, a new Pontiac Firebird Trans Am had a base MSRP of $7,135 before any fees or options.
The Black & Gold Special Edition Package (RPO Y82/Y84) was a $1,260 deal at the time, and it included the T-tops, gold cast-aluminum snowflake wheels, black-and-gold striping and decals, and the gold interior accents on the dashboard, steering wheel, and door panels.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube From the moment Vagner parked the car in his shop, Benjamin took over. With the vehicle up on a lift, he inspected the underside with a flashlight. He stopped at the front, where he noticed silicone that did not come from the factory leaking out at the seam of the timing cover, along with a massive oil leak.
Someone had already worked on that area, taking off the distributor cap and marking the rotor and the pulley with chalk to check the timing chain. They had likely suspected the stretched timing chain had jumped a tooth.
Expectedly, the 400-cubic-inch Pontiac W72 V8 is a no-runner. It has been hibernating for roughly four decades, but when it did run, it pumped out 220 horsepower (223 metric horsepower) and 320 pound-feet (434 Newton meters) of torque.
That made the F-body Pontiac Firebird Trans Am flash from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 6.7 seconds on its way to a top speed of 126 mph (203 kph). The Borg-Warner Super T-10 four-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube Vagner is well aware that if the 400 V8 needs a rebuild, it is going to cost him around $6,000. But before he makes any move, he needs to remove all the dust and grease from the engine bay. In the meantime, he does some research and finds out that the model was recalled for fan blade replacement.
Flexible cooling fans that equipped the 1978 Firebird Trans Am were designed with thinner steel blades that flattened out at highway speeds to reduce drag and save fuel. Over time, normal engine vibration and flexing caused metal fatigue and hairline stress cracks around the central hub or rivets, which could allow a blade to break off while the engine was running.
Benjamin takes the front end apart to access the internals. Removing the cover reveals that three plastic teeth from the aluminum timing gear were missing. No wonder this car was parked and never driven again. The mechanic realizes that someone at the service shop had slapped on a cheap replacement chain simply to get the Trans Am out the door.
So from this moment on, Benjamin can either replace the chain and the gears for around $130 or rebuild the entire front assembly, including a new water pump and timing cover, for about $800. He will also need to work on the brakes and replace the brake fluid, which has gone the color of coffee after sitting for so long in the reservoir. Expectedly, the engine oil has gone black and thick. No surprise there, either.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube After hours of hard work, the V8 roars back to life and sounds like it longed for the road. " It stays with me until it drives the miles that the dealership never drove, " says Vagner. He paid just $15,000 to take it home. On the collector market, Black & Gold Special Editions (Y82/Y84) average $68,000 to $85,000.

There’s a Brand New Toyota Corolla Cross on the Horizon, Is This What It Will Look Like?
6 photos
Photo: Kolesa
While the current Corolla Cross recently stepped into the 2027 model year in the United States of America, with revised pricing and fewer hybrid trim levels, Toyota is preparing the second generation of its compact crossover, as the model has turned out to be successful.
Rumor has it that the upcoming one might premiere either in 2027 or maybe in 2028, depending on whom you ask, and if it is a case of the former rather then the latter, than the current model year will be the last of the first generation. However, we think that it might be due in 2028, so it could be a 2029 model by the time it reaches our shores.
Recent information coming from Japan claims that the next-generation Toyota Corolla Cross will grow in size, getting closer to the RAV4. The GR Sport variant should be a thing, with a more aggressive design on the outside, some changes in the cabin, and likely a sharper chassis setup, and due to the rumored larger size, the interior should be a lot more spacious compared to the current one.
We recently saw a camouflaged tester of the upcoming model, though reports speak of a minimalist interior layout, and an exterior design perhaps influenced by the Toyota Corolla Concept shown late last year. This is pretty much the approach taken by Kolesa’s Nikita Chuyko, who stands behind the renderings shared in the gallery.
Photo: Kolesa This imagined new-gen 2028 or 2029 Toyota Corolla Cross somewhat looks like an enlarged C-HR. It features an entirely new front fascia compared to its predecessor. The hammerhead-styled headlights are new, there’s a light strip spanning across its entire width, and new headlights mounted further below and on the outer edges of the bumper, which has more discreet vents on the sides and a slightly smaller air intake in the middle.
The side windows are shorter, there are new lines running across its sides, and a quite Jaguar-like rear lighting signature, this writer believes. The CGI model features thin taillights that span into the rear three-quarter panels, and they are linked together in the middle of the tailgate by a light strip. The tailgate is decorated with the Corolla emblem in the middle, and no longer features a recess for the license plate, as this was moved to the redesigned bumper.
Toyota’s next-gen Corolla Cross definitely looks more upscale in these renderings compared to today’s model, and it is definitely not bad at all. We expect it to pack several electrified powertrain options, though details about it remain unknown for now. And before wrapping it up, we have to ask you whether you fancy this rendered new Corolla Cross more than the current one. So, do you?
